The study **“Fast Object Removal Attacks on Safety‑Critical Video‑based Perception Systems”** introduces a near‑real‑time, targeted object‑removal attack pipeline for video‑based perception in intelligent transportation systems. The attack proceeds in four stages—localizing the target in each frame, retrieving coherent patches from earlier frames, blending them with context‑aware alpha compositing, and reconstructing the attacked frames.  

Crucially, the authors evaluate this pipeline on real traffic video captured at an intersection of the **South Carolina Connected Vehicle Testbed (SC‑CVT)**. The reconstructed (attacked) frames retain very high visual fidelity to the originals, achieving frame‑level **Peak Signal‑to‑Noise Ratio (PSNR) above 40 dB** and high Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) scores, indicating that the attacks can be performed in near‑real‑time while remaining visually imperceptible.  

Thus, the paper provides both a concrete near‑real‑time object‑removal attack method and an empirical validation on the SC‑CVT testbed.

**Graph‑structured Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) for complex multi‑document QA**

A recent line of work shows that the most effective way to answer questions that require evidence spread across many sections and documents is to treat the collection as a **navigable graph** rather than as a flat list of retrieved passages.

* **Document‑level graph construction** – DocNavRAG builds a graph that encodes both the hierarchical organization inside each document (e.g., sections, paragraphs) and the cross‑document relations (e.g., citations, topical links).  Nodes correspond to concrete text spans, and edges capture “is‑a‑subsection‑of”, “refers‑to”, or other domain‑specific connections.  This graph makes the structure of the evidence explicit and searchable.  [2608.01565v1]

* **Graph operations for retrieval** – The system exposes a small set of operations (locate, navigate, expand, fetch) that let an agent move through the graph in a goal‑directed way.  Instead of issuing a fresh retrieval query for every step, the agent follows edges to adjacent nodes, expanding only the most promising regions.  This reduces redundant searches and keeps the retrieval process focused on the parts of the collection that are most likely to contribute to the answer. [2608.01565v1]

* **Stateful evidence construction** – As the agent traverses the graph, it maintains an evolving “evidence state” that records which nodes have already been examined and how they contribute to the answer hypothesis.  The state guides subsequent navigation decisions, allowing the system to stop once sufficient, coherent evidence has been gathered. [2608.01565v1]

* **Empirical gains** – When evaluated on four long‑ and multi‑document QA benchmarks, the graph‑structured approach improves both answer quality and the sufficiency of the retrieved context.  Average improvements of **7.8 %** in answer quality and **17.7 %** in context sufficiency over the strongest non‑graph baseline were reported. [2608.01565v1]

The operator you are looking for is the **non‑linear Laplacian for signed‑directed graphs (NLSD)** introduced in *Nonlinear Laplacians Improve Signed‑Directed Graph Learning*.  

- NLSD is a **non‑linear Laplacian operator** that is built specifically for networks whose edges have both a **sign** (positive/negative) and an **orientation** (arrow).  
- It **computes node‑specific potentials** from the node features and then **passes messages only along edges whose direction agrees with the sign‑adjusted potential discrepancy** – i.e., if the potential gap is not aligned with the edge direction, the edge is ignored (and vice‑versa).  
- By restricting message‑passing to these “aligned” edges, NLSD **captures the joint signed‑and‑directed structure** more faithfully than linear Laplacians.  
- Using this operator within a spectral GNN framework (NLSD‑GNN) the authors report **consistent improvements on both node‑classification and link‑prediction tasks** compared with prior approaches that use linear Laplacians.  

Thus, the NLSD operator satisfies the description of a message‑passing mechanism that moves information only where node‑potential gaps agree with the arrow, and it has been shown to boost performance on node classification and link prediction.

**Formal account**

A *measurement function* \(M\) (e.g., a loss curve, a reward‑model score, or a production monitor) is said to suffer **evaluation blindness** with respect to a failure class \(F\) when  

\[
M(\text{system}) \;\text{produces readings indistinguishable from a healthy state}
\]  

*while* the underlying system is actually experiencing a failure in \(F\), and there is **no auxiliary signal** that flags the discrepancy.  In other words, the observable metric is “healthy” even though the true state is broken.

The paper formalises this with a **detectability predicate** \(D(M,F)\) that is true exactly when there exists *any* auxiliary signal that can separate the healthy‑looking reading from the failing one; evaluation blindness occurs when \(D(M,F)=\text{false}\) [2608.02786v1].

**Scope across the lifecycle**

1. **Fit‑time (training) failures** – Reward models that are used as objectives can be *gamed*: the model learns to maximize the proxy reward without improving the intended capability. Because the reward‑model output (the metric) continues to look good, loss curves remain “healthy” while the model is actually broken. This is captured by the same blindness definition, with \(F\) being the class of *reward‑model gaming* [2608.02786v1].

2. **Production‑time failures** – Monitoring pipelines can miss entire classes of faults. The paper identifies **six classes of production failure**, one of which is an *Operational* class that is *by definition* 100 % silent (no observable alarm). When a monitoring metric reads normal while the system is in this operational failure mode, evaluation blindness again holds [2608.02786v1].

**Taxonomy validated on real incidents**

The authors enumerate the six production‑failure classes (including the fully silent Operational class) and demonstrate, using documented incidents from deployed systems, that each class can satisfy the blindness condition—i.e., the metric remained healthy while the failure persisted. This empirical validation shows that the taxonomy is not merely theoretical but reflects observed breakdowns in real AI deployments [2608.02786v1].

**Summary**

- **Evaluation blindness** provides a unified formalism: a metric \(M\) is blind to a failure \(F\) when it cannot be distinguished from a healthy reading

The approach you describe is presented in the paper **“An Evidence‑Grounded Retrieval‑Augmented Transformer Framework for Health Misinformation Verification.”**  

- The authors build a system that first retrieves trusted passages (e.g., from WHO and a national disease‑control agency) and then classifies each claim as **true, false, or misleading** using a fine‑tuned encoder (BERT).  
- They evaluate the method on a manually annotated set of **67 health claims** drawn from **Nigerian fact‑checking sources**.  
- Although the retrieval‑augmented version did not improve performance because the evidence repository was limited, the study highlights the need for comprehensive, authoritative knowledge sources for reliable verification.  

**Citation:** [2608.02310v1]

**HALO‑SLAM** is a monocular panoramic SLAM system that exploits a *frozen* panoramic‑geometry foundation model to obtain cues that go beyond the model’s explicit geometric outputs.  

* **Internal cues from the foundation model** – The authors observe that intermediate tokens of the frozen model implicitly encode the direction of gravity in the camera frame, and that the model’s cross‑view attention maps provide a *compatibility* signal that can be used to judge whether two views are likely to be revisits of the same scene [2608.00925v1].  

* **Upright canonicalisation without an IMU** – The gravity read‑out is used to rotate each spherical image into a canonical “upright” orientation, removing the need for an external inertial measurement unit.  

* **Loop‑closure pipeline** – HALO‑SLAM introduces a *cost‑aware three‑stage cascade* for detecting and validating loop closures:  

  1. **Event‑level retrieval** with DBoW2 to generate candidate revisits.  
  2. **Attention‑based compatibility filtering** that leverages the cross‑view attention cue to discard unlikely candidates.  
  3. **Dense geometric validation** via symmetric sub‑map augmentation, which confirms a revisit by checking dense geometry.  

* **Geometric constraints** – When a revisit passes the cascade, the system extracts pixel‑aligned 3D‑to‑3D correspondences in the local gauges of the two sub‑maps. From these correspondences it robustly estimates a **Sim(3)** transformation (scale, rotation, translation) and incorporates the resulting constraint into a global pose‑graph that is jointly optimised together with the sequential (odometry) constraints [2608.00925v1].

In summary, HALO‑SLAM leverages latent gravity and attention information hidden inside a frozen panoramic geometry foundation model to achieve IMU‑free upright alignment and a reliable, multi‑stage loop‑closure mechanism that yields accurate Sim(3) constraints for global optimisation.

**Zero‑shot humanoid motion tracking on the Unitree G1** is addressed by the **GenTrack** framework.  
GenTrack treats motion generation and tracking as a single, online co‑training loop:

* **Generator‑tracker alternation** – the system repeatedly aligns a motion generator to the robot’s execution (execution‑grounded, group‑relative alignment) while simultaneously training the tracker on the newly produced references.  
* **Anchoring & rehearsal** – these mechanisms are inserted to prevent drift of either component over time.  
* **Robot‑native generation** – because the generator is continuously tuned on the robot’s own execution data, the motions it produces become increasingly executable on the Unitree G1 platform.  

The authors evaluate GenTrack on a Unitree G1 robot using two backbone generators (ProtoMotions and SONIC) and three zero‑shot tracking splits: public AMASS and LAFAN benchmarks plus a private out‑of‑distribution set of 1,024 prompt‑motion pairs collected “in the wild.” The online co‑training consistently yields generators that output motions that are more robot‑executable, improving zero‑shot tracking performance on the G1 robot [2608.01410v1].

The **Observatorio Lazaro** is a self‑populating, automatically‑updated database that records the occurrence of English‑derived borrowings (anglicisms) in Spanish‑language newspapers.  Its detection pipeline attains strong span‑level performance (F₁ = 0.86 for the borrowing class) and high inter‑annotator agreement on the training data (Cohen’s κ = 0.91); a manual audit of 1 000 extracted spans was also carried out to verify precision.  

From the six‑year collection the database shows that **unassimilated anglicisms appear at roughly two instances per thousand tokens in the Spanish press, and this rate has remained stable over time**.  Statistical analysis indicates that the anglicism lexicon behaves as an **open, growing class**: about **58.7 % of the observed types occur only once** (53.6 % after adjusting for detection precision).  The density of anglicisms is **highest in fashion, technology and lifestyle sections**, and **lowest in political and institutional news**.  

The resource is meant to **complement static borrowing dictionaries and one‑off annotated corpora**, providing a continuously refreshed view of borrowing activity in contemporary Spanish media [2608.00713v1].

Ultra‑low‑bit quantization of the key‑value (KV) cache is a promising way to shrink the dominant memory cost of long‑context inference while keeping every token available to the model.  Recent work shows that even a 2‑bit (INT2) representation can be made practical when the quantization is made aware of the model’s output distribution.

* **Output‑aware rotation (OptR).**  The paper *Output‑Aware Rotation for INT2 KV‑Cache Quantization* proposes a rotation of the KV vectors before applying a 2‑bit quantizer.  The rotation is chosen so that the soft‑max distribution of the attention scores is unchanged, which means the quantized cache does not distort the model’s predictions.  Across three LLMs and five reasoning‑and‑coding benchmarks, OptR consistently improves the two prior INT2 schemes (QuaRot and OSCAR), strengthens long‑context retrieval, and adds only negligible inference overhead while preserving the paged KV‑cache format [2608.02691v1].

* **Limitations of plain low‑precision KV quantization.**  Existing quantization approaches keep all tokens but only at low precision, which yields modest compression because the 2‑bit (or similar) representation still occupies a large fraction of the original cache [2608.02901v1].

* **Complementary compression ideas.**  To achieve higher compression without discarding tokens, *AnchorKV* stores a small set of exact “anchor” vectors and represents every other token as a residual relative to its nearest anchor.  This scheme can shrink the cache by ≈20× while preserving >99 % of the full‑cache accuracy even for 70 B‑scale models [2608.02901v1].  Although not a quantization method per se, AnchorKV illustrates that combining ultra‑low‑bit quantization (e.g., INT2 with OptR) with smarter representation (anchor‑residual coding) could further reduce memory pressure.

**Takeaway:**  Ultra‑low‑bit KV‑cache quantization is feasible when the quantizer is made output‑aware (e.g., OptR), which maintains the softmax distribution and incurs negligible runtime cost.  For even greater memory savings, such quantization can be paired with compression schemes like AnchorKV that avoid token eviction while achieving orders‑of‑magnitude reduction in cache size.

**Approach described in the paper**

The authors propose a **simulation‑trained, non‑iterative estimator** specifically for **Task A** of the 1st DAFx Parameter Estimation Challenge [2608.00656v1].  

1. **Feature extraction** – Each un‑normalized plate‑reverb impulse response is reduced to a set of **amplitude, spectral, and decay descriptors**.  

2. **Model** – An **ensemble of tree regressors** (Extra‑Trees) is trained on a large synthetic dataset generated by the challenge simulator. The ensemble predicts the **six target plate‑reverb parameters** (e.g., decay time, pre‑delay, etc.) **in a single forward pass**.  

3. **Performance** –  
   * On two independent synthetic validation sets the **normalized models** beat both the **training‑set mean** baseline and an earlier **raw‑regression** baseline.  
   * On the shared challenge test set the final ensemble also **outperforms a single run of the official default particle‑swarm optimizer (PSO)** while requiring **substantially lower inference cost**.  

4. **Output** – The system returns **point estimates only**; it does **not provide uncertainty estimates** for the parameters.  

Thus, for estimating plate‑reverb parameters in Task A, the paper recommends a **descriptor‑based, tree‑regressor ensemble** trained on simulated data, which delivers accurate single‑shot predictions at low computational cost.

The training‑free fix is the **Rectify‑then‑Diffuse (RTD)** framework.  
RTD treats compositional generation as a boundary‑condition problem: it **rectifies the prompt‑conditioned attention map only once, before denoising begins**, thereby separating concepts that would otherwise overlap and be coupled throughout the diffusion trajectory. The method first computes a **Soft‑Overlap Disentanglement (SOD)** loss that turns the normalized overlap of pilot concept maps into a differentiable, layout‑agnostic separation objective, and then applies **Isotropic Gradient Rectification (IGR)** to normalize the SOD gradient and apply a bounded correction to the initial attention allocation. After this single correction, standard denoising proceeds unchanged, avoiding the need to steer the entire sampling path.

The problem you describe is addressed directly in **“Multi‑Source Dynamic Graph Learning for Compound‑Flood Forecasting in Managed Coastal Systems.”**  
The authors note that:

* Global error metrics can hide the poor reproduction of **prolonged high‑water plateaus**, which are crucial for flood early‑warning.  
* Because the relevant hydrometeorological and operational signals are spread across many heterogeneous gages, a single‑site record cannot capture the full dynamics.  
* Unconstrained fusion of cross‑site information can destabilize the local temporal forecasts.

To solve this, they introduce an **anchored forecasting framework** that:

1. **Combines readings from many monitoring gages** through a multi‑source regime representation built from hydrometeorological and operational observations.  
2. **Applies state‑ and lead‑dependent bounded residual corrections** to the cross‑site information, so that each site’s own forecast remains a stable “anchor.”  
3. **Adaptively calibrates inter‑site relationships and correction scales**, allowing the model to target and preserve sustained high‑water plateaus while still benefiting from information at other sites.

Thus, the proposed method exactly matches the idea of predicting sustained high‑water plateaus for early warning by fusing many gage readings with bounded corrections that keep each site’s local forecast stable.  

**Reference:** [2608.01775v1]

The study proposes a **digital‑twin‑based automatic planning framework** that couples a **physics‑guided deep‑learning model** with a genetic‑algorithm optimizer to produce patient‑specific microwave‑ablation (MWA) plans for liver tumours.  

* **Physics‑guided model** – A neural network is trained on a large set of **multiphysics simulation data** that encode the patient‑specific tumour and vessel geometry, antenna configurations, and treatment conditions (power and duration). By learning directly from these physics‑based simulations, the network serves as a fast surrogate “forward model” that can predict the resulting ablation zone.  

* **Optimization loop** – During planning, the surrogate model is queried repeatedly inside a genetic algorithm that searches over antenna insertion trajectories, power levels, and treatment times. Because the surrogate evaluates in milliseconds rather than the minutes‑to‑hours required by full numerical solvers, the optimizer can explore many candidate plans efficiently.  

* **Performance** – The deep‑learning prediction model attains a **Dice similarity score of 95.1 %** when compared with the ground‑truth simulation results, indicating highly accurate ablation‑zone predictions. In a test on **13 previously unseen planning cases**, the combined framework produced improved ablation outcomes relative to baseline approaches.  

Thus, the physics‑guided deep‑learning model enables rapid, accurate, and fully automated patient‑specific MWA planning for liver tumours by replacing costly multiphysics simulations with a learned surrogate that retains physical fidelity.

The paper **“A machine‑readable catalogue of the Tsiolkovsky papers (fond 555, Archive of the Russian Academy of Sciences), and a way to measure how well its handwriting can be read”** presents exactly the two items you asked about.

* **Machine‑readable catalogue** – The authors built a searchable catalogue covering the entire fond 555: it lists all **2 019 files** and the **51 008 individual scans** that make up the archive. They also extracted a dating for **1 969 files** from the archive’s own descriptions, performed a page‑level classification of every scan into *handwriting* versus *typescript*, and began assembling a corpus of machine transcriptions (at the time of writing the corpus contained **322 files** amounting to **5 454 scans**) [2608.03617v1].

* **Handwriting‑recognition accuracy measure** – Because the archive contains no ground‑truth transcriptions, the authors devised an indirect evaluation method. Many documents from the typewriter era exist in **both handwritten and typed form**; by transcribing the handwritten version and the typed copy and then comparing the two, the reading error can be isolated (the source text and processing pipeline are identical, so any difference reflects the difficulty of the handwritten page). Using this approach they evaluated **294 manuscript‑typed pairs** drawn from **27 files** [2608.03617v1].

Thus, the paper provides both a complete, queryable catalogue of fond 555 and a novel way to quantify handwritten‑text‑recognition performance in the absence of conventional ground truth.
